questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-4y={e}^{4x}.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below. 

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-4{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{4x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{4x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{4x})}^{′}-4(u{e}^{4x}) & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+4u{e}^{4x}-4u{e}^{4x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x}+\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}}-\cancel{4u{e}^{4x}} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{4x} & ={e}^{4x} \\ {u}^{′} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =1 \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ u & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{4x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{4x} \\  & =x{e}^{4x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3y=5.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-3{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{3x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{3x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{3x})}^{′}-3(u{e}^{3x}) & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+3u{e}^{3x}-3u{e}^{3x} & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x}+\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}}-\cancel{3u{e}^{3x}} & =5 \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{3x} & =5 \\ {u}^{′} & =5{e}^{-3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =5{e}^{-3x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 5{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =-\frac{5}{3}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{3x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{3x} \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}{e}^{-3x}\cdot {e}^{3x} \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y=\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}+2{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-2x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{-2x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{-2x})}^{′}+2(u{e}^{-2x}) & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-2u{e}^{-2x}+2u{e}^{-2x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x}-\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}}+\cancel{2u{e}^{-2x}} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ {u}^{′} & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & ={e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x \\ u & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{-2x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{-2x} \\  & =\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x\cdot {e}^{-2x} \\  & ={e}^{-2x}\int {e}^{2x}\operatorname{sinh}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the first-order linear ODE

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-5y=10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x.
$$

We wish to solve this equation using the method of variation of parameters (VOP).

Select the correct options below.

$\,$ According to VOP, we assume a particular solution of the form {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Solving for $u,$ we have $u(x)=$ {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the particular solution is ${y}_{p}(x)=$ {{field-3}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

To find the complementary solution ${y}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
{y}_{c}^{′}-5{y}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving this equation, we find that the complementary solution is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{5x}
$$

where $A$ is an arbitrary constant.

The method of variation of parameters constructs a particular solution by varying the constant in the homogeneous solution. So, to find a suitable ${y}_{p},$ we set $A=u(x)$ in the complementary solution, as given by the following ansatz:

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=u(x){e}^{5x}
$$

Intuitively, this form of ${y}_{p}$ tracks the homogeneous solution but with a varying amplitude.

To find $u,$ we substitute our ansatz into the equation, apply the product rule to the derivative term, and simplify to isolate ${u}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{(u{e}^{5x})}^{′}-5(u{e}^{5x}) & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+5u{e}^{5x}-5u{e}^{5x} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x}+\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}}-\cancel{5u{e}^{5x}} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′}{e}^{5x} & =10\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\ {u}^{′} & =10{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x=\frac{{e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}}{2}
$$

our equation for $u$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =10{e}^{-5x}\operatorname{cosh}⁡5x \\  & =10{e}^{-5x}(\frac{{e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}}{2}) \\  & =5{e}^{-5x}({e}^{5x}+{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =5+5{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$ (omitting the arbitrary constant), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′} & =5+5{e}^{-10x} \\ \int {u}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =\int 5+5{e}^{-10x}\,\text{d}x \\ u & =5x-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-10x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since ${y}_{p}=u(x){e}^{5x},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & =u(x){e}^{5x} \\  & =5x{e}^{5x}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-5x}.\end{aligned}
$$
